report.answer_text:
The Mars flyby (March 1, 2025)
Gravity assist: Europa Clipper passed just 550 miles (884 km) above Mars' surface. The maneuver bent its trajectory to set up the next leg of its trip to the Jupiter system.[1] It was moving at about 24.5 km/s relative to the Sun at closest approach and left at about 22.5 km/s.[2] Mars' gravity slowed it and reshaped its solar orbit.
Thermal imaging: For about 18 minutes, the E-THEMIS thermal imager captured one image of Mars per second.[3] The flyby was used to calibrate the infrared imager and carry out other science tests.[3]
Radar test: The spacecraft also tested the components of its radar instrument together for the first time.[3] The REASON radar bounced signals off Mars. This was the first full test of an antenna system too large to try on the ground.[4]
Arrival at Jupiter
Europa Clipper is due to reach Jupiter in April 2030. Several sources give April 11, 2030[5] as the date. Before that, it will make an Earth gravity assist in December 2026[6], planned for December 3. After arrival, the flybys of Europa are planned to start in 2031[6], and the mission will make 49 close passes of the moon.
